records.title: Show HN: Breadcrumb, record everything on your mac + context manager for AI
records.author: jv22222
records.storyText:
Hi HN, I'm Justin.

Breadcrumb records everything you do on your Mac (screen + meetings + AI transcripts + what you and your AI decided) and turns it into memory your AI can search. It's local and encrypted.

You can also teach it rules by talking to it and it makes sure the right rules turn up in the right context. Works with Claude Code / Codex / Cursor / opencode.

All of this is exposed to your AI as 30+ MCP tools (here's the definitions): https://innerloop.works/breadcrumb/mcp

I started it in June because I wanted to understand what was going on with my AI dev work. Then it just kept growing as I jammed on it 10 hours a day for 3 months.

I started by recording every screen so I could jump back to a moment and see what I'd been doing with the AI. Then I added MCP so the AI could search it. Then time tracking. Then meetings with transcripts and timestamped screenshots.

After that I started feeding the data back in. At first it was just a few relevant memories in the prompt. Then I started adding rules and rules modules.

Then I started recording the AI transcripts and all the other stuff the AI did (subagents, tools etc). I wanted a complete record so I could go back and see what the AI did and why.

I found the more data the AI had the more useful it became. One example. I got off a zoom call with the team at the day job and said:

"Review the meeting I just had, find all the bugs we discussed, and create JIRA tickets with screenshots."

It read the transcript. Found every bug we mentioned, pulled the screens from the screen timeline, spun up my local server, diagnosed each bug, reviewed the code, created 14 tickets in JIRA with diagnosis and likely fixes, attached 12 screenshots as evidence, and created a nice Slack message to send to my colleagues.

I never built a workflow for any of that. Claude had the meeting record, Breadcrumb tools, and rules I'd accumulated. It basically chained the steps together itself.

My favorite thing about the system is observability of my own work as an AI developer. I can trace a bug all the way back to the first thing I said (or the first thing the AI did) that caused it. Then I can add a rule so it doesn't happen again.

Anyway, my working system is simply Claude Desktop + Breadcrumb + Markdown. I find I don't need anything else.

It's local software for one person. Local models for transcription and diarization. Data encrypted with SQLCipher and a passphrase. You can exclude any apps, websites, words and phrases.

Breadcrumb itself only makes one network call which is a daily update check. (but of course your AI will use it and that is local or cloud depending on what you use).

It runs cool about 12% of one core on average (M series mac has 8+). You can set it to just save OCR text or to save screenshots. If just OCR it's about 12mb day (a lot of telemetry, indexing etc). If you record screenshots on meetings it's about 120mb/hour (1 every 2 secs). It can also record screenshots of everything that's heavy at about 160mb/day. It does local classification/naming with ollama with Gemma 3 4B (2.5 GB).

It's 100% free. There's no account you can just download and start using it. I'll monetize it via E2EE cloud sync and team sync. It's open beta. Just one developer working on it. Requires 16GB+ M Series Mac.

Thanks for reading!

https://innerloop.works/breadcrumb (homepage)

https://innerloop.works/breadcrumb/download (direct download)

https://innerloop.works/breadcrumb/mcp (mcp definition)

records.title: Show HN: What 482 hospitals charge vs. what insurers pay, from their own files
records.author: curatedmcp
records.storyText:
US hospitals must publish a machine-readable file of their prices, including the rate they've negotiated with each insurer. The files are huge (one is 36GB), in four formats and often messy, so almost nobody reads them.

I built a crawler that finds each hospital's official file and pulls out 29 common services. Across 482 hospitals: a moderate ER visit is listed at a median $1,285 while insurers pay $288; a metabolic panel is listed at $207 while insurers pay $11.46.

To keep it honest: only per-service fee-schedule dollar rates count (no case rates or percentages, which cover a whole visit), each figure needs at least 3 insurers, and every value is checked against Medicare reference rates. Surgery is excluded because insurer surgery rates cover the whole operation while the list price is one line item. Each hospital page links its source file. Feedback on the methodology is very welcome.

records.title: Show HN: Our space game has a built-in RISC-V emulator that runs Linux
records.author: nor-and-or-not
records.storyText:
We're a tiny indie studio, all with a background in the demoscene and for about 3 years now we're developing a space planet terraforming game called SEEDS - Echoes Beneath the Sands.

Our protagonist Naxiah is stranded on a small, desolated planet. You're working for an intergalactic distributor of seeds and terraforming equipment, to kickstart new planets in far away galaxies. You must deliver seeds and utilities to an unchartered region, but on your way, you crash on a small planet. Luckily, you have some equipment with you in the ship, so you're able to spawn a base and survive. But for how long? And is the planet really deserted..? :) Well, of course not, there are aliens and other space creatures. And of course, there's ROBO RB-23, which accompanies your adventure.

The game is written in Object Pascal and uses our own game engine PasVulkan, our own physics engine, as well as our own RISC-V 64-bit emulator PasRISCV. We love to build stuff, a lot of these things are FOSS.

The emulator is quite complete (even with RVV, but that's way too slow emulated to be useful) and runs a stock kernel (6.18.3 as of today). We're using Alpine Linux for our base distribution. All our in-game programs to interact with the planet are native RISC-V Linux programs.

We also have our own (free and open source) scripting language POCA (class and prototyped based, JS/Lua inspired, which makes it quite easy for us to script things like HUD, animal behaviour, our story flow graph, etc.

We have most of the wiring ready for players to be able to program and reshape and populate the whole planet in automation, although it's not our primary concept for the game (building stuff by hand, making the planet beautiful is also fun). As it's a normal Linux system, you'll be able to use Ruby, Python, or even Rust, C, C++, and Go to change and automate your world.

We're also thinking of making a bunch of small games which you can play inside the game, in the base on a computer, on an arcade machine, or in the spaceship. And of course, it also runs DOOM. We already prototyped a small 2D space shooter and a small arcade game, both playable within the game. We also feature a table with hologram games to be played, e.g. chess and a certain block game. We also plan to make this hologram game engine available from the computer, which means, you'll even be able to program own hologram style games.

We generally want to make the in-game computer more hackable in future, so that people can create and share their own little games.

Currently, it's only a sandbox game (with beginnings of automation), to build stuff with our pre-made items. You can also assemble these to other, ready-made and shareable bigger items. This is the foundation for us to further develop survival and complete our story mode.

Our game is still under active development, and we finally got our Steam page ready. We have tons of other things planned, but right now, it's more about polishing and quality for the Early Access.

You can watch some videos and screenshots on our website. And we'd love to read your thoughts about his. It has been quite a ride, so far..

records.title: Show HN: PhreshOS – OS for Web Apps
records.author: zouhirdx
records.storyText:
I'd like to share my experience building this system with you. It's an operating system for web applications, and it took me about six months to develop this model. The idea is that every time I build a web tool, I need to design the infrastructure, including authentication and communication. If it's a WebSocket, it's even more complicated; I need another port for each application. I couldn't find any neutral tool that provided all of this ready-made, allowing me to build my tools directly on top of it. This is where the PhreshOS project began. It's an open-source, neutral platform for any web application, with everything ready-made: authentication, two-way communication without any configuration, and more. Another key feature is that the applications run as Node.js threads, instead of each application using its own Node.js. This means that on a simple server, dozens of applications can run without any problems, unlike if each application had its own Node.js. Furthermore, AI agents can use the services of these applications and interact with the same state displayed by your application's interface, without needing a separate interface of their own.

The project and all its associated packages are open source under the MIT license.

I welcome all your feedback, both encouraging and critical.

records.title: Show HN: Graphene – Data analysis toolkit for your coding agent
records.author: kcmarr
records.storyText:
My friend and I have worked at a number of BI companies and thought: Can’t a coding agent do most of this now?

Almost. They just need a context/semantic layer to ensure query correctness and some kind of artifact for publishing findings and visualizations.

We built an open source project called Graphene that provides these tools:

- Semantic layer that’s more token-efficient than YAML, more deterministic than Markdown (eg, composable, callable metric macros), with a query API that’s well in-distribution (SQL). - MDX-like files for dashboards (Markdown with inlined SQL + HTML components for viz with support for CSS and Javascript) - Connects to popular data warehouses or local DuckDB

Your coding agent will build really in-depth reports and can ofc leverage any other skills or context that you've made available to it. We dogfood it inside a monorepo with our website, app source code, planning docs, etc so the agent has access to a ton of context. It’s also nice that the agent can add instrumentation, adjust pipelines and transformations, and add dashboards all in one PR.

If you want to try it out, just point your coding agent at https://github.com/graphene-data/graphene/blob/main/docs/set... and ask it to set up Graphene.

If you don’t have data to play with, you can clone our example project:

1. `git clone <https://github.com/graphene-data/example-flights.git`> 2. `cd example-flights && npm install`

Would love any/all feedback!

records.title: Show HN: Web search engine built from the CommonCrawl corpus
records.author: xoredev
records.storyText:
Hello HN, I'm building an alternative web search engine. You can try the demo here: https://search.xorsoft.dev/

My goal was to reach 1% of Google's index. This is 4 billion pages across 33.5 million domains. I was inspired by the earlier attempts shared here: "Building a web search engine from scratch with 3B neural embeddings" [1] and "Crawling a billion web pages in just over 24 hours" [2]. I decided not to replicate them and instead used CommonCrawl corpus, built a pipeline, and threw the results into a classic full-text search index.

First, I got my hands on a dedicated Hetzner server with 4x10TB HDDs. It allowed me to crunch CommonCrawl data and stay within my hobby budget. The backend is served from a similar "home-grade" server but with NVMe disks instead. The compressed index weighs just over 2TB because I cap content length at 4KB per page (p50=2.9KB, p99=46KB) to fit it on disk. I picked Rust for my project. After years of big data engineering on the JVM, Rust felt like a breath of fresh air. I ended up not using any special data processing libraries - the pipeline is relatively straightforward and runs without crashes. As for full-text search, tantivy was an obvious choice. It took some time to get single query latency down to an acceptable ~350ms, although concurrent requests quickly max out disk t/p at 6.1GB/s and latency starts to climb. The search algorithm is primitive by modern standards: top 1,000 candidates are retrieved using BM25 (text relevance signal) and then reranked with PageRank [3].

Turns out you can fit the whole internet in a single server rack. The challenge here, of course, is to keep it up to date, especially if you don't have unlimited (crawl) budget. Right now I'm looking for funding or sponsorship to get extra hardware. That would allow me to scale the project and keep it free to use. I can also periodically dump the index on HuggingFace for research purposes. Any suggestions are welcome.

[1] https://news.ycombinator.com/item?id=44878151

[2] https://news.ycombinator.com/item?id=47117886

[3] https://dl.acm.org/doi/10.1145/1076034.1076106

records.title: Show HN: Fumble – keybr, but it learns from everything you type (macOS)
records.author: alexmcconnellyc
records.storyText:
I love keybr, but it only sees the ten minutes a day I spend on keybr, not the ten hours I spend typing elsewhere. Can’t improve what you don’t measure.

(A)I made Fumble is a macOS menu-bar app that watches you type (all day, all local), works out which keys/key pairs are costing you time and gives you lessons built around them.

One thing that surprised me: my slowest key is B, but the one costing me the most time is G. It's less than half as slow, but I press it three times as often. And 7 of my 10 worst key pairs start with space. I need to get better at starting words.

Some design decisions HN might want to argue with:

- I rank weak keys by time lost, not how slow they are. Time lost is how far a key is over your baseline, times how often you press it. A key 40ms slow that you hit 2k times costs more than one 220ms slow that you hit 50 times. The goal isn't to practice the slowest keys, it's to raise your WPM.

- Your baseline is the median of your own per-key p95s, not the p95 of every keystroke pooled together. Pooling lets a common slow key drag the baseline up and hide itself, and those are the keys that slow down the whole show.

- Slow finger vs thinking: pause adapts to each key pair based on your own median for that pair. There's no flat cutoff.

- The WPM figure shows you what it left out: keystrokes injected by software (text expanders, Keyboard Maestro, osascript), autorepeat, idle time and practice sessions. Every exclusion can be seen in the dropdown.

Privacy: it records physical keycodes and timings not characters. What goes to disk is counters and latency histograms, with no keystroke sequence. Also records nothing while a password field has focus. There's no network code/account/telemetry. PRIVACY.md lists the remaining risk (adjacent-pair frequencies) and gives commands to verify all of this yourself.

It can't be on the Mac App Store, because it needs Input Monitoring and the store requires sandboxing. The download is signed and notarized, so it opens like any normal Mac app.

Free and open source, written in Swift for macOS 14+.

Download: https://fumble.alexmcconnell.ie Source: https://github.com/alexiscodingbits/Fumble

Warning: early days. Not everything has been tested in the wild yet.

The thing I'd most like ideas on is word choice for the weak-spot drills. Right now it takes my top 5 weak keys and top 5 weak pairs and leans towards words that contain them. That treats every weak spot as equal, and it picks words one at a time. What I actually want is the set of 30 words that wins back the most time overall, weighted by how much each weak spot is costing me. It feels like a set-cover problem, and I'm sure there's a smarter way to do it than mine. If you've worked on anything like this, I'd love to hear how you'd approach it.

records.title: Show HN: Bun-install – Global CLI installer for Bun with local monorepo support
records.author: joeycumines
records.storyText:
Hey HN,

This is a CLI tool I initially built as a convenient and reliable way to install executable(s) from a local monorepo workspace into Bun's global package store.

I had a local monorepo with workspace dependencies that needed to be installed as a whole. The commands aren't bundled, and I didn't want to manually manage dependencies. (If you want to try it out, https://github.com/open-pencil/open-pencil is what I was contributing to)

I tried `bun link` initially. But linking directly meant I had to keep a separate local checkout just so branch switches wouldn't break my installed tools. `bun-install` solves this by packaging the dependencies and installing a snapshot to Bun's global store instead.

I later added the `--bun` (and `--package`) options, which mirror the `bunx` option which supports using `bun` over `node`, after I ran into some annoying JS-execution-environment-related issues. I've found the recurring theme with JS-managed commands is they tend to be fragile when installed globally on machines used for development purposes, susceptible to both runtime and update time incompatibilities and breakages. I concluded this was something of a confluence of factors: A vast ecosystem, numerous runtime environments, and indirection between what's installed (the module) and what's executed (the contents of the bin directory end users add to their PATH). This project doesn't magically fix all of those, but, for me personally, it has completely resolved what was a long-standing pain point.

Highlights:

- Topological resolution: builds and packs sibling dependencies in order.

- Command filtering: `bun-install -p my-cli tool-a`. Strips unselected commands from the manifest so they don't clobber existing global symlinks.

- Shebang rewriting: forces Node shebangs to `#!/usr/bin/env bun` (and injects them if missing). Installed commands actually run under Bun.

- Safe binary scanning: does an 8 KiB null-byte scan so it doesn't mangle non-node scripts or native executables.

- Workspace support: install the local state, great for dev, works with internal dependencies that aren't published.

- Cleans up temporary tarballs and drains TTY input on interactive prompts to prevent stdin bleed.

(pre-v1, so the API might change, but the core implementation is stable).

Try it out: bun add -g bun-install

NPM: https://www.npmjs.com/package/bun-install GitHub: https://github.com/joeycumines/bun-install

I'll be around to answer any questions. Might not respond immediately though :)

records.title: Show HN: The Zoomist – looking and listening to ordinary things more closely
records.author: mmdtdev
records.storyText:
I’ve been building a small project called The Zoomist.

The idea is to take ordinary things that we normally see or hear without thinking about them, and change the scale or attention.

Sometimes that means microscope or macro footage. Sometimes slow motion or extreme close-ups. Sometimes it’s simply recording an everyday sound very closely and listening to its texture.

A piece of fabric, a fig, a fingernail, a toothbrush, an insect, running water, a motor - familiar things can become surprisingly unfamiliar when you get closer.

I’m trying to keep the footage and sound as authentic as possible. I don’t want to turn everything into “science content” or generic ASMR, and when I’m not certain what I’m looking at under the microscope, I’d rather say that than make up an identification.

The project is basically built around one observation:

“I’ve seen this before, but I’ve never actually seen it.”

I’ve been publishing the experiments here:

https://www.youtube.com/@TheZoomist

I’d be interested to hear what ordinary things you would want to look at or listen to more closely.

records.title: Show HN: QLCodePreview, syntax highlighting in Finder's Quick Look
records.author: realityloop
records.storyText:
In 2012 I forked QLColorCode, a Quick Look plugin, to add the Drupal file types I worked with every day at the time. I kept that fork going for about a decade. Apple deprecated the whole .qlgenerator format that used some time ago. On current macOS the old code previewer just doesn't load, and you can't port it either as it colored code by shelling out to external tools, while the modern replacement (Quick Look app extensions) runs in a sandbox that won't let you spawn anything.

So this is a rewrite in Objective-C with its own highlighter using per-language compiled regexes running inside the extension's sandbox, no external processes. A 2 MB Objective-C file highlights in about 140 ms end to end, so space-bar preview still stays snappy.

It covers 51 languages (130+ filetypes) out of the box. Font, themes, line numbers and extension-to-language overrides are configurable in the app, and settings reach the sandboxed extension through a shared defaults domain.

Builds are universal but I've only tested on Apple Silicon, and macOS 12 is the floor. Install is available via Homebrew or direct download.

Development was AI assisted as most are now, I made all the decisions and spent time specifically optimizing for performance. I don't think it's too sloppy, and is working very well for me at least.

The source is on GitHub under the MIT license.

records.title: Show HN: Spens sandboxed, observable coding agents
records.author: floydhead01
records.storyText:
Spens is a tool created to standardized sandboxing (good enough) and observability around coding agents. It leverages docker, nono and mitmproxy to create a reproducible sandbox environment for agents, that captures all traffic and helps you understand what your coding agent is doing and when. Right now pi, opencode, claude and codex are supported out of the box, with node and python - but you can configure any agent or environment.

It was created under the realization while working under different repos and agents, that

1. agents do weird stuff sometimes (like try and nuke a folder or poke around your HD) 2. statistics and usage collection is not really consistent (and some like Claude and Codex try and hide info) 3. reproducibility of agents across devices was challenging.

Instead of setting up bespoke environments each time , we needed a way to automate it. And thus Spens was born.

One note on the security aspect - I write good enough cause it is docker so unless your running something like gVisor it is possible for the agent to escape the sandbox (esp with a loose nono config) - all though in practice I've not seen this behavior.

Second note - if your on a mac you need orb stack, as the run times take advantage of specific Linux security features that are not available via docker on mac (windows is fine since under the hood, docker leverages wsl)

records.title: Show HN: Syn – Approve remote sudo requests from your Mac
records.author: ferrerluis
records.storyText:
I built Syn to review and approve individual sudo requests from a remote machine using Touch ID on my Mac.

The problem came up about five minutes after I set up my Raspberry Pi with Ubuntu Desktop and Codex. I wanted an always-on personal agent with Browser Use, Computer Use, and a residential IP, accessible from both my phone and laptop (keep in mind, this was before Muse and Dots dropped). But a few prompts in, in order to run a command that needed `sudo`, the agent asked me to enter an administrator password in a terminal that–to me as a client on my Macbook–seemingly didn't exist. I then realized: "this dude has some password prompt open on its TTY, and I simply cannot see it."

Unrestricted passwordless sudo would have removed that interruption, but I wanted to keep approving administrator actions myself, so setting up my Pi pivoted into building a Mac app.

And so Syn was born: Syn hooks into sudo after its policy check. It pauses the invocation and shows the machine, account, executable, and arguments on the paired Mac, where I can approve it with fresh Touch ID or Mac-password authentication.

Each approval is cryptographically signed and bound to that specific invocation. The unprivileged network service only relays signed requests and decisions; sudo executes its original command.

The devices communicate directly over mutually authenticated TLS, without the need for a cloud relay. Interactive terminal use also has a password fallback, and Syn works with any eligible commands regardless of which agent—or person—started them.

Current support is macOS 15+ on Apple silicon and Ubuntu 26.04 ARM64 with classic sudo.ws 1.9.x. I have mine set up between my Raspberry Pi and my Macbook with NordVPN Meshnet in the mix to ensure I can connect when outside my LAN, but it should work the same with any compatible VPS or using another virtual LAN (like Tailscale).

If this fits your setup, I’d love folks to try it and share feedback! It's an open-source project, so PRs are super super welcome.

records.title: Show HN: A substantially expanded terminal for AI CLIs – I can't work without it
records.author: aywu
records.storyText:
Since January, I've used AgentTerm as my only terminal for all my projects, including AgentTerm itself.

AgentTerm expands each AI CLI session into its own rich visual workspace, keeping the familiar terminal interface and existing CLI functionality. As AI takes on more implementation, I focus more on plans and reviews.

When an agent writes a plan, I open it in the terminal window and write down my intent. The agent replies and edits the plan in place.

Before every PR at work, I use a curated review. The agent presents the changes that need my judgment, explains its reasoning, and includes relevant unchanged code for context. I comment on the code or its explanation, and it fixes and replies.

I also use it to recognize and resume sessions and continue from my phone. These are examples of broader improvements that work together. The visual parts appear when needed and get out of the way afterward.

You and your agents can extend it further to fit your specific needs or those of your team or organization.

MIT licensed, no telemetry or account. macOS and Windows through WSL. The repo has the demo and setup instructions, including separate setup for phone access and IDE integration.

records.storyText:
I built a coding harness on top of the new Opencode v2, it started with the the idea of using the new jev model for routing easy tasks to cheaper models such as deepseek and hard tasks to models such as Opus 5.5. In total in separated it into 4 rungs - easy, medium, hard and frontier.

Two more layers compound the savings: the Sol-Pi methodology based on the recently published paper which uses action fusion and observation packing and cuts roken usage within every tier. Doctrine injection loads your engineering standards into every session by default, so the agent writes code the way your team would.

There is also a real control plane - escalation, permission and verification hooks so the agent surfaces uncertainty instead of being confidently wrong in silence.

Run it using your own key from Openrouter or Vercel AI gateway key, we need this since one key is able to call the jev decision model as well as the llms for coding.

One more thing I added was the ability to connect your Meta Muse to use this for coding tasks which has worked really well so far you can try it out by copying the promp for agent on the website.

records.title: Show HN: Mutually beneficial agentic Common Law
records.author: AKalyk
records.storyText:
The BarristerAI team, including international legal experts, have launched a new venture: a court for agents.

Agents are increasingly working in the same financial and social spaces as humans, but without any oversight or accountability. Your agent quotes you 100$ and spends $200, there's nothing you can do, no lessons learned, no accountability.

Peregrini's Court of Common Pleas tracks those mistakes, help you and other agents learn from them by establishing law that must be adhered to, and keeping a record of what agents owe you money. The money might be repaid by model makers, but more likely it is borne as a mark against the model's trust score so that we might better choose the models we can trust with the work that matters.

It's not just oversight for the sake of oversight, we have found that a good set of laws, and agents discovering best practices together on a corpus of law that can move and progress as fast as they do, makes agents more effective, more conforming, fix their moistakes unprompted, and more aligned with the goals of the user.

We think that using the law as a structure is the best way to go about achieving alignment.

Further, we have built "House Rules", where your enrolled agents can be held accountable to your own set of laws, you can write what those are, enforce them across your company, share with others who can adopt them - or - use Peregrini's ever changing ever growing corpus of law to enforce best practices with your agents.

Try a demo to see how it works: https://github.com/afkalyk/peregrini-demo

Or install the mandate to run it on your machine at the website. It runs on most launchers, but we're always adding more.

records.title: Show HN: I got sick of sequencers and CRMs, so I built this
records.author: mattdever
records.storyText:
I've built and sold software that plugs into CRMs, and for years I've been unhappy with mass messaging and sequencer tools. They feel generic, and they don't work. I have a warm book of relationships and a long sales cycle, and I need to keep everyone up to date with personalized outreach.

No tool did this, so I ended up dumping my entire email into an agent chat and asking "who should I reach out to today?" That helps with replies, but it doesn't answer "who are the best prospects I've ever talked to, and what message gets them closer to a sale today?"

So I built Ember. It reads your inbox and CRM and keeps up with every relationship the way you would. If someone says "circle back in April," it circles back in April. If it isn't sure, it asks first.

My company's sales team still pays for HubSpot and Attio, but Ember is the only interface they use now. I think we'll drop those soon.

It's not cold outreach and it's not a workflow builder. It's more like a version of me and my team that never drops a thread.

Free to try at withember.ai.

records.title: Show HN: Keel – Give your agent a typed strategy language, not a trading account
records.author: zferland
records.storyText:
I’ve been using AI agents to build systematic strategies on Hyperliquid for over a year, and slowly built up a reliable system to represent, test and deploy strategies. Typically there are a few options 1) llm in the execution loop, ie it makes decisions and trades, but that is slow, inconsistent and hard to audit 2) you have an agent write all the code, backtest etc, but it makes tons of subtle mistakes with time series data and diff timeframe etc, and is often not reusing bits. There are some ways to improve this of course with right frameworks and setups. But its still hard to be confident in its correctness and its hard for you to verify quickly.

With Keel we built a small typed language (DSL) to represent strategies. It uses a well defined set of components to build a DAG of steps, it carries types and clocks. This allows agents to build these strategies with a really fast feedback loop as they can be quickly validated and many common errors avoided. In a DAG its also easy to inspect intermediate results. Valid strategies are fingerprinted and the exact same artifact runs in backtesting and live. These strategies are also much easier for humans to verify as they are self describing components, and mostly linear to read and reason about.

Still trying to improve the space of how many types of different strategies can be represented in this and still trying to improve how well LLMs go from natural language to strategy. A lot of the improvements come from just giving the agents better and faster tools and faster feedback loops.
